title: Judge extends block on Trump White House ban of MS NOW, CNN and Politico
content: A federal judge late Tuesday night indefinitely extended his block on the White House from enforcing a ban on three media outlets that President Donald Trump announced in mid-September. The preliminary injunction by Judge Timothy Kelly replaces his temporary restraining order against Trump's ban of MS NOW , CNN and Politico from the White House complex as a lawsuit challenging the ban plays out. "President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him," wrote Kelly, who was nominated by Trump for his seat in U.S. District Court in Washington. In his written opinion, Kelly said the three outlets were likely to succeed on their claim in their pending lawsuit, which argues they were denied due process when Trump summarily barred them without giving them a chance to argue against it. The judge cited two existing opinions by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which establish a due process right to journalists whose White House passes are targeted for revocation. Those appellate opinions are binding on federal District Court judges in D.C. The judge also said, for the first time in this case, the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which allege retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. Kelly's order Tuesday is not a final ruling on the merits of the suit. And it does not compel the White House to restore access to the Oval Office and Air Force One to the outlets. Kelly brushed aside the Department of Justice's claim that in addition to concerns about inaccurate news stories, Trump decided to revoke the outlets' access to the White House on national security grounds. "There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote. The judge said the DOJ's national security argument appears to be "merely a post-hoc justification for the decision" after the outlets sued. MS NOW reported Wednesday that the DOJ declined to comment on the ruling. "Still, no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed," Kelly wrote. "That said, for the reasons explained below, the Court will extend the relief it already ordered, which will continue to preserve the status quo while this case proceeds," Kelly said, referring to his prior order that restored access by the outlets to the White House. The judge said that without the preliminary injunction, the outlets were "likely to suffer irreparable harm." His ruling came on the heels of a court hearing last Thursday, when the DOJ defended the ban, which reportedly led to 78 journalists having their so-called hard passes to the White House revoked before Kelly ordered them restored with his previous temporary restraining order. Trump last month said he would appeal any decision by Kelly blocking his ban. CNBC has requested comment from the White House and DOJ. Theodore Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, said in a statement, "We are grateful that the Court ruled in favor of our clients." "When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said. "Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers." "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," the attorney said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this "unconstitutional ban on the free press" for the foreseeable future." Trump on Sept. 18 said that he was banning the three outlets because of how they have covered him. In a Truth Social post that day, Trump wrote that the outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America." Trump later said that same day that he had become "sick" of "cumulative stories" by the outlets. The ban took effect on the following day, Sept. 19, when journalists from the outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their permanent passes confiscated by Secret Service officers. The outlets sued Trump on Sept. 21 in a civil complaint that said, "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles." Kelly, two days later, issued a restraining order that temporarily reversed the ban for at least 14 days. Journalists from the three outlets on Sept. 24 were allowed to return to the White House, and since then Kelly extended the restraining order to allow him time to consider whether to issue Tuesday's preliminary injunction, which has no set expiration date. — Justin Papp contributed to this report.

title: Everyone has weighed in on the Shane Gillis monologue controversy, except ‘SNL’
content: As anger builds online against comedian Shane Gillis’ description of women as “whores” during his “Saturday Night Live” monologue, one party is staying noticeably absent from the conversation: “SNL” itself. The show and its network NBC haven’t commented publicly on the backlash, nor have they responded to requests for comment. It’s a familiar playbook for “SNL,” which has often chosen to stay mum and ride out the waves of controversy that have punctured its decades-long run. The backlash over Gillis’ monologue was, perhaps, predictable. The Philadelphia-born comic was previously fired from his role as a cast member, just a few days after his hiring was announced, after clips emerged of him using an ethnic slur against Chinese people and a mock Asian accent on his podcast, as well as gay slurs. By way of explanation, he offered that he was a “comedian who pushes boundaries.” Gillis’ return to the series as a guest host last weekend saw him in classic form, styling himself as a beer-swilling bro, an everyman who shirks political correctness. He hasn’t been to the gym in a while, he said during his “SNL” monologue, so he should be forgiven for being surprised by how women dress to work out now: “Like whores.” “Look, I’m sorry. There’s no other way to describe it,” he said. They wear tight shorts, he said, with the color of “artificial bait.” “SNL” and its longtime boss Lorne Michaels – have often stayed quiet after hosts or their comments attracted backlash, never commenting, for example, on the controversy over Dave Chappelle, who has hosted the show twice since being criticized for transphobic comments he made in 2021. While “SNL” is staying quiet, others are speaking out — both in and outside 30 Rock. For Jessie Leo, a graphic designer who works on the long-running sketch comedy show, Gillis’ comment wasn’t just offensive. It was also indicative of an unsafe workplace. “How am I ever supposed to feel comfortable going to NBC HR after knowing the company and people I work for gave the thumbs up for Shane’s whore joke during his monologue,” she wrote on Instagram late Tuesday. “In general, but especially at a time like this with rape culture and victim-blaming assailing women from all angles right now.” Cecily Strong, who was the longest-tenured female cast member in “SNL” history, excoriated Gillis’ cruel characterization of women on her own Instagram story. “On my way to Pilates in my new slutty ass orange shoes and rainbow socks,” she wrote above a picture of her legs in workout gear. “Might sell sex on the way not sure.” Former “SNL” cast member Ego Nwodim cast her own shade at Gillis, writing “whore reporting for duty” on a picture of herself dressed for the gym earlier this week. On TikTok, too, dozens of women have posted images of their gym outfits with references to Gillis’ comment. Outside of “SNL”-world, “Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy made a minute-and-a-half video about the monologue, saying, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists.” He called out other men, too. “More men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime,’” he said. Like many of Gillis’ critics, Strong highlighted the timing of Gillis’ monologue. As Gillis was joking about women dressed like “whores” and working out at his friend Joe Rogan’s private gym, less than 200 miles north an investigation was unfolding into the alleged gang rape of a former undergraduate at Cornell University. The investigation into the 2024 incident, triggered after the former undergraduate filed a lawsuit, unleashed outrage and a flood of women to share similar stories of sexual violence and abuse.

title: Joni Mitchell is now an American citizen, six decades after moving to the US
content: Joni Mitchell has finally become an American citizen, more than 60 years after leaving her native Canada . The legendary singer-songwriter posted a picture of herself holding a US flag at the naturalization ceremony on Tuesday, with the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.” In the image shared with her more than 1 million Instagram followers, a smiling Mitchell wore a red beret and sunglasses, and extra stars and stripes pinned to her cardigan lapel. Mitchell, who turns 83 next month and was using a walking stick, also posted a short video clip from the ceremony, in which she was applauded by others gathered in the room. Born in Fort Macleod in Alberta, Canada, in 1943, Mitchell will continue to have a Canadian passport as both countries allow residents to hold dual citizenship. The iconic artist, who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 and won a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Grammys in 2002, is best known for 1970s hits such as “Big Yellow Taxi,” “Blue,” “Amelia” and “Woodstock.” She studied commercial art in Alberta before moving to Toronto in 1964, where she performed at local folk club and coffee houses. Then, during a brief marriage to folk singer Chuck Mitchell, she lived in Detroit before eventually relocating to New York City. It was there that she made her eponymous album, also known as “Song to a Seagull.” Mitchell, who has 19 studio albums and six live records to her name, later moved to Los Angeles, where she settled in the city’s Laurel Canyon before later moving to Bel Air. It is unclear why Mitchell chose this time, when relations between Canada and the US are particularly strained, to become an American. She was widely reported to have taken a swipe at President Donald Trump while performing at the Hollywood Bowl ahead of the last presidential election in 2024. According to media reports at the time, the noted protest singer encouraged her audience to go to the polls: “Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote — I’m Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.” Mitchell has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, including a stroke and a brain aneurysm in 2015. Her health setbacks did not stop her from performing at the 2024 Grammys, where she won the award for best folk album for her 2023 release “Joni Mitchell at Newport.” This year she also received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Junos, Canada’s equivalent of the Grammys. An as yet untitled biopic of Mitchell’s life is said to be in development, with IMDb listing Cameron Crowe as the director and Meryl Streep in the starring role.

title: Gustavo Dudamel arrives in New York with a mission that goes beyond the podium
content: It was a star-studded gathering at Lincoln Center , with the likes of Steven Spielberg and Alec Baldwin toasting New York’s new Philharmonic director with champagne, arepas and the din of salsa music. It’s been a while since the city’s cultural elite has buzzed as it has with the arrival of Gustavo Dudamel, 45. Dudamel, or “The Dude,” as he was known during his 17 season-run at the helm of the Los Angeles Philharmonic , was a force in LA, both on the stage and in his efforts at tackling the age-old issue of democratizing an artform often seen as elitist. Dudamel broadened the Philharmonic’s reach through educational programs and crossovers with popular culture, notably appearing at the halftime show at the FIFA World Cup final , and conducting scores for films like “West Side Story” and “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” Now, he has arrived in New York with a similar mission, and has spoken from the beginning of his belief that music is a “fundamental right.” “You really have to take the risk,” Dudamel said in an interview this summer. “To really make people feel that they belong.” Dudamel’s sensibility was forged as a child growing up in the Venezuelan city of Barquisimeto, where he learned to play violin through El Sistema, Venezuela’s National System of Youth and Children’s Orchestras and Choirs. The program was founded in 1975 by José Antonio Abreu, a musician and economist who believed that classical music — long reserved for a select few — could transform the lives of Venezuela’s poorest children. Since its founding, more than one million people, according to official Venezuelan figures, have taken part in the program, which operates in community centers and offers free instruments and lessons to children, most of whom come from low-income families. “What my colleagues in Venezuela understand about music is that it’s not just decorative, it’s not just extracurricular, and it’s not just fun, although it is fun,” said Anne Fitzgibbon, founder and executive director of the Harmony Program , a New York City nonprofit that provides free music education to children in underserved communities. Fitzgibbon drew inspiration to create the program after studying El Sistema in Venezuela on a Fulbright fellowship in 2007. El Sistema was founded decades before Hugo Chavez came to power in a populist revolution that quickly turned authoritarian. He and his successor, Nicolás Maduro, continued funding the program, and so its ties to the state have drawn scrutiny. For years, critics also questioned Dudamel’s silence about Chavez and Maduro and the human rights abuses and corruption that marked their reins. Dudamel broke his silence in May 2017 after a young musician was killed during a protest. “I raise my voice against any form of repression,” he wrote at the time in an open letter . “Times cannot be defined by the blood of our people.” Speaking to CNN this summer, Dudamel praised El Sistema. “It’s not a musical factory system,” he said. “El Sistema is using music to transform the lives of children.” Dudamel has landed in a city with several programs inspired by El Sistema’s model. Around the US, some 150 organizations inspired by El Sistema — ranging from community programs to YOLA , the youth orchestra Dudamel helped found in Los Angeles — teach music to more than 30,000 students, according to El Sistema USA , the network that connects them. Carlos Sánchez was just 13 when he first performed alongside Dudamel at a concert in his native Maracaibo, Venezuela’s second biggest city. Years later, after studying bass through El Sistema, he toured the world with the Simón Bolívar Symphony Orchestra under Dudamel’s baton. Now he is the director of UpBeat NYC , a community music center in the South Bronx offering free music education for 230 students aged 5 to 21. “When I first came to UpBeat, I saw how the program worked with the children. It was what I was feeling back in my country,” Sánchez said. Funded by private donations and grants, UpBeat also helps families with food and support during difficult times. “It’s not just asking a kid whether they practiced,” said Sánchez. “It’s asking, ‘Are you hungry? Is everything okay at home?’” Now, groups like UpBeat hope Dudamel’s arrival will bring more attention to them and allow them to grow. “He’s bringing power to a few levels that we’re interested to see how he utilizes,” said Richard Miller, the program’s co-founder and co-executive director. “We’re going to be there trying to be in his ear to make sure it’s going to the families that we represent and work with.” Following Dudamel’s appointment, the Philharmonic’s co-chairman, Oscar L. Tang, and his wife, Agnes Hsu-Tang, donated $40 million to advance music education and bring orchestra to new audiences. “In our generation, we’ve not had a music director that has been both equally committed to what’s happening at the podium, as he is with what is happening in the schools,” said Gary Padmore, the New York Philharmonic’s Vice President for Education and Community Engagement. Padmore acknowledged that New York’s school system remains deeply segregated and said his team is targeting the city’s “arts deserts,” such as Corona in Queens and Canarsie in Brooklyn. Change will take time, he said. Dudamel will be with the orchestra for only about 15 weeks a year, and Padmore described a conductor’s first season as a period of “deep listening.” Miller, of UpBeat, tempered his enthusiasm with caution. The issues run deep — he noted that the orchestra must still diversify and that Afro-Latino artists fought for decades to broaden classical music’s audience and that Lincoln Center itself was built on San Juan Hill, a neighborhood whose Black and Puerto Rican families were displaced to make way for it. A few miles from Lincoln Center, Sánchez said he hoped Dudamel would inspire UpBeat’s students, just as the conductor once inspired a young Sánchez in Maracaibo. “I didn’t know any of this until they came to me,” he said. “I hope with all my heart that he can come and bring the same hope.”

title: Danny Dyer in floating poo water protest on Thames
content:
Actor Danny Dyer has delivered a petition to Downing Street calling for water companies to be nationalised after floating a giant poo sculpture down the River Thames on a boat.
Dyer and Sittingbourne and Sheppey MP Kevin McKenna sailed along the Thames with the sculpture as part of a protest calling for the water industry to be brought into public ownership.
The actor, who runs a caravan park on the Isle of Sheppey with daughter Dani Dyer, delivered the petition having previously joined a local sewage protest in Leysdown in September .
A government spokesperson said it would "give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible".
Nearly 350,000 people have signed the petition, started by campaigners SOS Whitstable.
Rivals actor Dyer and his daughter, who is currently competing on Strictly Come Dancing, joined the protest in September alongside singer Becky Hill, and Surfers Against Sewage.
He previously called the quality of bathing water "a disgrace", adding that issues with sewage discharges were "a very dangerous thing".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he wants to see "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors, but suggestions that water companies could be nationalised have received pushback, including from lenders to Thames Water .
A government spokesperson said the prime minister had been "clear that the failures of the past must be corrected".
It added: "We are bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."
According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025.
There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states.
Speaking outside Downing Street, McKenna told the BBC: "What you see is what you get with Danny, he is a man of passion and he is determined to do this.
"He has been meeting with a lot of local people who have shown him the scale of the problem.
"The vast majority of the public is really sick of it [sewage discharges] - they want it ended, I want it ended, and Danny wants it ended."
A spokesperson for trade body Water UK said it was working to end sewage discharges "as fast as we possibly can".
Southern Water, which supplies water to the Isle of Sheppey, said it was "tackling the root causes of pollution through our record £8.9bn investment programme" and cut pollution incidents by almost a third between 2023 and 2025.
"No pollution is acceptable and we're working as fast as possible to bring about the improvements our customers expect", it added.

title: BBC director general defends plan to shelve new Archers studio
content:
The BBC's director general has defended the decision not to record The Archers at its flagship new Birmingham headquarters - and said options were still being explored to keep it in the West Midlands.
Plans to build a bespoke studio for the long-running Radio 4 soap at the corporation's new Tea Factory building, in Digbeth, were shelved this week as part of a wider drive to cut costs.
Matt Brittin, who met with West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker on Wednesday, said the broadcaster needed to save money but they were working together to look at future recording locations.
"We're going to explore how we can best house The Archers where they need to be and at the moment, we have other studio space around the country which could accommodate them," he said.
The Equity entertainment union said cast members were "angry at the proposals and will fight them".
The drama, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year.
Brittin said The Archers was "going strong and... going nowhere" but acknowledged the BBC was "living in financial constraints" and had to make £500m worth of savings.
"So what we've said is, we're not going to build a £1.5m bespoke studio for that production, which is something we might have afforded previously.
"But what we are going to do is make sure The Archers continues to exist here."
The region's mayor Richard Parker has said he was disappointed by the news and wanted the recording to remain in the city.
"The Archers was born in Birmingham and is a key part of our broadcasting heritage," he wrote in a statement on Tuesday.
"We have the talent and the facilities here. There is no good reason why we should lose a programme that has called Birmingham home for decades."
Speaking to the BBC, he added: "We've now got the fastest growing creative economy in the country with increasing large amounts of programmes being produced here.
"I understand the financial pressure the BBC is under, but my responsibility is to this region and protecting and growing our creative sector here.
"The BBC is critical to that and I've made it really clear to the Director General that, whilst I understand the challenges he faces, I also want to secure and retain investment here."
Equity said the proposal was short-sighted and would leave the West Midlands, and the BBC, poorer.
Actor Tony Turner, who plays Vince Casey in the soap, said the proposals were troubling.
He said the show's history meant it had "a commitment to Birmingham, and we're proud of that, and we'd like to stay here".
Speaking during a visit to the BBC's current Birmingham base at the Mailbox, Brittin described the programme as "magic" and said there was still time to explore other options before the broadcaster moved to the new Tea Factory site in 2028.
"We shouldn't really go behind the curtain, but we need a drama studio and that's different from a radio studio normally, and we've got others that we could use," he said.

title: Racial bias in London music licensing, report says
content:
Black-led music events in London face disproportionate restrictions and cancellations because of "racial bias" in licensing and policing, a report has concluded.
The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report , commissioned by the Greater London Authority, said that black-led events were blocked at higher rates than white-led events in the capital, and South Asian-led events also faced restrictions.
The report said genres including Afrobeats, hip-hop, drill, R&B and dancehall were routinely flagged as "high risk", while indie, pop and rock nights faced less scrutiny.
Cameron Leslie, chairman of the mayor's London Nightlife Taskforce, welcomed the report and its recommendations.
The Metropolitan Police said it understood the "concerns and differing views" on the matter, and would "carefully consider the report's findings".
London Councils, which represents local authorities across London, has been asked for comment.
The report, carried out by Black Lives in Music, was informed by interviews, focus groups, workshops, a survey and internet research. Freedom of Information (FOI) requests were also submitted but were largely rejected or only partially answered.
Researchers said that a lack of race-disaggregated licensing data (data broken down into racial and ethnic categories), limited official datasets and rejected FOIs made some patterns difficult to measure.
Alongside black-led events, the report also looked at South Asian-led events, but found that South Asian music was "largely invisible within licensing records".
The report suggested that South Asian music and cultural events were often allowed to proceed through "negotiation, modified hours and conditions", but said the evidence did not demonstrate that South Asian music was "disproportionately cancelled" in the capital, and incomplete licensing records made firm conclusions difficult.
The report was welcomed by the Musicians' Union, UK Music, the Music Venue Trust, the Night Time Industries Association and LIVE trust, among other organisations.
Dr Hakeem Stevens, report co-author and lead researcher, said they looked back to the beginning of recorded sound in the late 1800s as part of the research.
"We've got incidents of licensing decision issues based around race going back that far - to the 1910s, 1900s and so forth," he said.
"People assume that the problems came about in the last 10 to 15 years," he said, adding that the issue dated back to approximately 100 years.
Issues dating back more than a century were not cited within the report, but the legacy of Form 696 was discussed.
The Metropolitan Police form, which was scrapped in 2017, had been dubbed a "racist" risk assessment.
It was introduced in 2005 after a spate of shootings at London club nights, and influenced similar forms used by other police forces in England .
The report said that licensing decisions for live music events were influenced by risk and "racialised assumptions about culture and safety".
The report said this meant that "institutional racism" was "reproduced" through routine processes rather than explicit bans or policies.
Event organisers and venue owners told researchers that "police intelligence" was "routinely used to justify heightened scrutiny of black and South Asian events", and gave examples of being asked to fund a police presence or private security for an event.

title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
content:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.
Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.
"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.
"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."
The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after doctors had found a rare benign tumour, called a colloid cyst, in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.
In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.
She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.
Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [the hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.
"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."
A year ago, for the first time since the brain surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.
According to the NHS , later stage symptoms of Alzheimer's disease include "significant problems with short and long-term memory".
Alzheimer's is a progressive disease and so symptoms gradually worsen over years.
After brain surgery, though, problems tend to be worst early on, then stabilise and improve over weeks to months. Some people are left with milder lasting changes.
Music therapy can help people to recover from brain injuries and McCall said she believes it was ultimately singing lessons that had "healed" her.
In April last year, McCall revealed she had been told - following MRI scans - that her tumour was "not coming back".
Benign tumours are not cancerous and they tend to grow slowly, according to the Brainstrust charity.
Non-cancerous brain tumours are more common in people over the age of 50, and symptoms can include headaches, vision problems and drowsiness, the NHS says.
McCall's surgery, known as a craniotomy, involved part of her skull being removed to take out the tumour.
She has spoken publicly about the procedure and her recovery before, including on Comic Relief and on her own podcast called Begin Again.

title: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture
content:
Telling the stories of three gay men across a century, this sweeping but relatively low-budget drama is second favourite to The Odyssey for the Academy's top prize. Here's why it could beat out Homer.
From the first 10 minutes of gay historical epic La Bola Negra, it's hard not to recognise you are seeing something very special. Opening with a scene of a sleepy Spanish village during the Civil War of the 1930s thrown into violence, it has a visual beauty and storytelling rhythm that are immediately spellbinding. It is inspired directly by the work of the revered early 20th-Century poet and playwright Federico Garcia Lorca, but also sprawls in other imaginative directions, creating a tapestry of memory, art and sexual repression across a century of Spanish life.
Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi's film tells the story of the lives of three gay men: Sebastian, in 1937, is a man who's been conscripted into Franco's army during the Spanish Civil War and is grappling with his love for a prisoner he is guarding. Carlos, in 1932, is a bourgeois twenty-something who's been rejected for membership of an exclusive casino club due to rumours of his sexuality. Alberto, in 2017, is a historian and researcher who comes into an unexpected inheritance from his estranged grandfather. La Bola Negra connects these stories in poignant and unexpected ways.
When the film first hit the Cannes Film Festival this May, the buzz around it inspired a bidding war between heavy-hitter distributors – an early sign that something special might be happening. Now being released by Netflix in North America, it is set to be a major Oscars contender. Odds makers put it at second favourite for best picture – meaning it could be set for a David and Goliath-esque battle with current favourite The Odyssey . Here's why it could even overcome the combined power of Homer and Christopher Nolan.
Since it premiered in Cannes, La Bola Negra has been a runaway hit with critics, regular audiences, and just about everyone in between. The Hollywood Reporter said it was "a sweeping, heartsick, often funny journey of recollection and fantasy. It is high time we had a gay war epic of this scope and soulfulness and invention."
It won best director for its film-making duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (tied with Polish director Pawel Pawlikowski), and went on to win the People's Choice Award at the Toronto Film Festival this autumn, too, which has been a common precursor for the Academy's best picture nominees and winners.
On top of this, it is proving a runaway commercial hit in its native Spain, with its box-office numbers actually increasing from its first to second weekend. All this is the kind of international recognition that makes the Academy sit up and take notice.
Mastering a complex triple-storyline structure across timelines is one mean feat. Blending multiple genres – romance, historical epic, family drama – is another. But at La Bola Negra's core throughout are its themes of gay desire, persecution and self-punishment. In the 1932 segment, there's a haunting story Carlos is told about a young gay man who was beaten to death and left to rot in a town square for 100 days. If the fear of homophobic violence rumbles under the surface of La Bola Negra throughout, the 2017 timeline also allows for reflection on it. Alberto scrolls Grindr and works on a project "on the margins of dissident desire".
More happily, La Bola Negra also takes seductive pleasure in scanning male bodies at play and rest: nude soldiers swimming in a stream, sailors smoking on city fences, tendrils of dark hair flopping elegantly over the eye. It shows courage in foregrounding sexual desire as much as it does persecution. As co-director Javier Ambrossi told Awards Watch: "A lot of our community is based in silence and pain... The movie encourages you to say: if you can do it, do not be a conformist, try to fall in love. Be happy, look for a spark." Twenty years have passed since another gay epic, Brokeback Mountain , was egregiously beaten to best picture by the now-unpopular Crash . A win for La Bola Negra could go some way to rectifying that mistake.
As Sebastian, musician and first-time actor Álvaro Lafuente Calvo – better known as Guitarricadelafuente – is remarkable. He has a sharp-planed, large-eyed look that can shift from openness to hunched paranoia by turns. It's perfect for a character whose traumatic past and constant fear of being discovered combine with a yearning sensitivity. As if this wasn't impressive enough, the star also made much of the original music for the soundtrack. Calvo and Ambrossi have discussed their preference for casting gay actors for gay roles , and were particular about doing so with this project. Carlos González is also excellent as the diffident 2017 character Alberto, who has a moving journey through his own family history across the course of the film. His scenes opposite veteran Pedro Almodóvar star Lola Dueñas, as his difficult mother, are wince-inducingly real.
The film also pulls in supporting performances from the international A-list, with Glenn Close as a US academic who helps Alberto on his research journey and, most memorably, Penélope Cruz, who performs an exuberant cabaret song for a bar of soldiers as a glamorous, freewheeling nightclub singer. It's a showstopping appearance that has put her in contention for a best supporting actress Oscar, but the backbone of the film remains the performances from the less experienced and/or well-known actors so carefully chosen by the film-makers. And, if the film's buzz continues to grow, there's hope that more than one of this ensemble may be nominated, which will hold it in good stead for the biggest award of Oscars night.
If La Bola Negra is proof of anything, it's that Calvo and Ambrossi know how to frame an image and make it sing. Lavish, ambitious, and formally daring, their film is heavenly to look at – shot on location in remote abandoned villages or in hyper-real sets. Shot by cinematographer Gris Jordana on 35mm film stock, each of the three stories has a distinct visual identity, taking cues not only from their settings but from the psychological framework of their protagonists. The camera lingers in a frozen overhead shot over a truck full of soldiers' corpses, full of blood and gore, until we see that someone there is alive. It glides beautifully through a smoky, darkened bar where Carlos drunkenly dances with strangers. And it sits static over a snowy field, stunning and melancholy, like a cinematic sigh.
The directors have discussed how the film was knowingly inspired by operatic Hollywood dramas and big-time Oscar-winners The English Patient and Titanic – which makes it all the more remarkable that all of this was achieved on a budget that came in under $20m (£15m). As Calvo said in an interview with El Pais : "a lot of people praise the film's classical sensibility… We're told it's the kind of film they don't make anymore." And that's exactly why it may appeal to Academy members.
La Bola Negra is released in US cinemas on 16 October and UK cinemas on 6 November

title: The Gentlemen star Ray Winstone charms locals in Welsh market town
content:
An actor renowned for his "hard man" image and London gangster roles looked at home filming on the more genteel streets of a south Wales market town.
Ray Winstone, recently seen in Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen, as well as star of The Departed and Sexy Beast, was spotted in Cowbridge in the Vale of Glamorgan, filming the six-part action-comedy Danger Money.
Winstone leads the cast as Alan "Razor" Sharp, an ex-SAS operative, with Cowbridge portraying a town in England.
"It created a real buzz," said Nadine Price, supervisor at Ground coffee shop on High Street, one of the filming locations.
Price said there was "real excitement" in the town, with Winstone spending time joking with residents.
The Welsh flag was taken down from the town hall for the filming, with Price saying Cowbridge would be depicted as a town in Herefordshire.
Winstone, 69, who was born in east London and is famous for his Cockney accent, walked the high street of Cowbridge wearing military medals and a flat cap in character as Sharp.
Winstone previously said his character was "a bit of a scrapper, surly and getting on a bit".
"I told them it doesn't ring any bells, but I like a challenge," he joked.
Molly Ridge, a stylist at Minnie May Closet, was about to film a promotional Instagram reel for the shop when she noticed the filming outside.
"I had one of our dresses on so I ran up to him and asked him for a selfie and he said 'yes of course babes, that's fine babes'. He was just really sweet.
"He said the dress looked gorgeous and I thought he could have been a bit off as he was just about to start filming but he wasn't."
She described Winstone as a "lovely man" who was "exactly the same in character as in real life with his proper gruff East End accent".
Anna Groom also works at the shop and asked for an autograph.
"He signed it to the 'Lovely Anna' which I thought was sweet and he came across like a really nice guy," she said.
Gary Simms, a Cowbridge local, also had a picture with the actor when he saw him in the Bear Hotel on Sunday evening, the night before filming.
"What a nice guy. We were watching [the] Liverpool-Man City game and we had a great chat about football, and he was wearing his West Ham joggers.
"It was surreal to see him in the pub as I'd just finished watching season two of The Gentlemen."
Winstone also recently appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, where his daughter, Jaime, is a contestant, sending a video message of support after she was in the dance off.
The comedian and actor faces charges including rape and sexual assault from six female complainants who have never met each other, a court is told.

title: Russell T Davies criticises BBC boss's 'clumsy' AI Doctor Who comments
content:
Longtime Doctor Who writer and showrunner Russell T Davies has criticised the new BBC director general over comments he made about an AI-generated episode of the show.
Matt Brittin told a Royal Television Society conference in September that he had been sent a "pretty good" 50-minute unofficial Doctor Who episode.
"That's a clumsy thing to say in an industry where he's got writers and artists and it specifically affects people, they're the first to take the blow," Davies told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show.
Addressing criticism he has received, Brittin told a staff meeting last week he was attempting to make a point around the "pace of change" while stressing he believed in "human creativity".
The director general joked he had "got into trouble" over what he had said, but added: "I was just trying to make the point: Look at the pace of change and what this stuff can do."
He said: "I want to be really clear: Humans are leading, and I believe in human creativity, enhanced by whatever tools."
He emphasised human-led creativity would always be at the heart of the BBC's mission.
But speaking to BBC Radio 4, Davies said that the new director general, who joined the BBC after a career at Google, "hasn't worked in television for that long and might not be so fruity with an opinion in future".
"My inbox went ping ping ping ping ping, so God knows what his was like," he added.
Davies was also asked more broadly about AI, including how, or if, writers should use the technology.
"I have heard stories of some writers using AI prompts to do a first draft which I find shocking because I think... What are you paid for otherwise? What are you there to do?"
He said he did not use it to write his scripts but he "very much" worried it would start to replace writers, and in some circumstances that may already be the case.
Davies is one of the UK's most influential television writers - from the ground-breaking Queer as Folk to acclaimed dramas including It's a Sin, Years and Years and, more recently, Tip Toe, he has had a major impact on British TV.
But perhaps his most significant achievement is his work on Doctor Who.
In 2005, he brought the Timelord back after a 16-year absence after pitching it to the BBC's then-head of drama at a party in Manchester.
He revived the show again in 2023, although he confirmed earlier this year he would be stepping away.
He told The Media Show there were times he "used to dread going on a Doctor Who set" because of the expensive special effects and "explosions going on, people pulling themselves in to prosthetics".
"It's more difficult than any other set."
The show is now at a crossroads.
The BBC cancelled the planned Christmas special and Disney+ no longer co-finances the series.

title: Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
content:
HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.
Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars –  shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells.
All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer.
"We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement.
"I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said.
"Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said.
Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting.
It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s.
The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century.
"We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said.
"To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."
The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".
Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.
In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.
In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival.
Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude.
"I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.
Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.
